meta.title: Who really said "It is better to die on your feet than to live on your knees"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: FDR used a version in a June 1941 message, but did not coin it. Quote Investigator traces this anonymous Spanish-language proverb to a Mexican article from 1906.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is better to die on your feet than to live on your knees'?
meta.ogDescription: FDR borrowed it in 1941, but the saying is an anonymous proverb. Its earliest close match is a 1906 Mexican article, and Zapata did not coin it either.

answer.label: Not Franklin D. Roosevelt — an older anonymous proverb
answer.sourceLine: Roosevelt did use a version of it, “would rather die on our feet than live on our knees,” in his June 19, 1941 message to a special Oxford convocation ↗. But Quote Investigator ↗ finds the saying in a Mexican article from 1906, already in quotation marks as a proverb, so whoever first said it is unknown.

source.heading: What Roosevelt actually wrote

docMeta.dd: Message to the Special Convocation of the University of Oxford
Read on his behalf by Maj. Gen. Edwin M. Watson at the convocation held at Harvard (per Quote Investigator)
El Mundo Ilustrado (Mexico), September 16, 1906, per Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: We, too, born to freedom, and believing in freedom, are willing to fight to maintain freedom. We, and all others who believe as deeply as we do, would rather die on our feet than live on our knees.
trail: Quote Investigator (April 16, 2026) ↗ names the 1906 article by Luciano J. Rivas as its earliest close match. The Spanish reads “vale más morir de pie que vivir de rodillas,” and because it is already in quotation marks, QI concludes that “the creator remains anonymous.”

The American Presidency Project text ↗ confirms that Roosevelt’s message of June 19, 1941 says “would rather die on our feet than live on our knees.” That is a borrowing, worded differently from the popular version.
Quote Investigator’s author also summarized the findings on the American Dialect Society mailing list ↗: the earliest match is 1906, and the Zapata, Aeschylus and Babeuf attributions are wrong.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line under Zapata, citing books from 1944, 1979 and 1988. It notes the line is sometimes misattributed to Che Guevara and to Dolores Ibárruri.
source.excerptNote: This is Roosevelt’s documented wording. The popular form, “It is better to die on your feet than to live on your knees,” is not what he wrote. That exact sentence does appear in Hemingway’s 1940 novel For Whom the Bell Tolls, where a character credits it to Pasionaria.

source.rightsNote: The popular English wording is an anonymous rendering of a Spanish-language proverb, and Quote Investigator’s earliest close match is a Mexican article from 1906. No identifiable author or translation can be tied to this exact sentence, so we assert no copyright status for it. Roosevelt’s 1941 message uses different wording and does not settle the question.

author.name: Anonymous proverb
author.heading: About Anonymous proverb
author.metaLine: Spanish-language proverb · earliest close match 1906, Mexico
author.bio: The saying “vale más morir de pie que vivir de rodillas” appears in quotation marks in a September 16, 1906 article by Luciano J. Rivas in the Mexican periodical El Mundo Ilustrado, which Quote Investigator takes as a sign it was already a proverb. It became linked with the followers of Emiliano Zapata and was popularized in Spain by Dolores Ibárruri (“La Pasionaria”) in 1936. Roosevelt and many others later picked it up.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why
misattribution.intro: Few lines have been pinned on as many famous people as this one. Quote Investigator lists Zapata, Ibárruri, Roosevelt, Hemingway, Aeschylus and Babeuf among the people credited, and none of them coined it.

items.why: His June 19, 1941 message to the Oxford convocation ↗ says “would rather die on our feet than live on our knees.” Major General Edwin M. Watson read it at Harvard. The saying was already in print as a proverb by 1906, and Roosevelt’s wording differs from the popular one.

Quote Investigator ↗ calls the Zapata attribution incorrect. A 1924 Survey Graphic article credited the saying to an anonymous follower who scratched it on a post after Zapata’s death in 1919, not to Zapata himself.

During the Spanish Civil War she made it famous in Spain. Quote Investigator ↗ cites the New York Times of October 2, 1936, reporting her words as “we would rather die on our feet than die on our knees.”

In For Whom the Bell Tolls (1940), the character Joaquín says “Pasionaria says it is better to die on your feet than to live on your knees.” Hemingway gives the line to Pasionaria, not to himself (QI ↗).

According to Quote Investigator ↗, the saying is not in the original texts. It comes from Robert Fagles’s 1975 English rendering of Agamemnon and John Anthony Scott’s 1964 English rendering of Babeuf’s 1797 trial defense.

misattribution.truthLine: Roosevelt borrowed the saying in 1941. It is an anonymous Spanish-language proverb whose earliest close match is a Mexican article from 1906 (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why Roosevelt reached for it
lead: In June 1941 the United States was not yet at war. Oxford University awarded Roosevelt an honorary degree at a special convocation held at Harvard, and the message he wrote for it argued that free inquiry and civil liberties were worth fighting for. In it he took up a saying that the Spanish Civil War had already made famous in English, and that Hemingway’s best-selling novel had repeated the year before.
So his use is real and documented, but borrowed. Each famous speaker who used the line helped it travel, and over time it came to be credited to whoever was quoting it.
